system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'.
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. For any measurement (e.g. BP, blood sugar, heart rate, lab values), briefly state what the normal range is and whether the patient's value was within it.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic given to fight the bacterial infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (a machine that cleaned the blood when the kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

output_text:
You are a 42-year-old man who came to {organization} on 26/12/2021. You stayed for 23 hours in the ward, and your bill was paid by sus. You came to the hospital on your own because it was an emergency and received hospital care.

You have Crohn's disease (a long-term condition that causes inflammation in your digestive system). You were admitted because you had abdominal sepsis (a very serious infection in your tummy) which was linked to your acute on chronic kidney disease (meaning your kidneys, which already had a long-term problem, suddenly got worse). You have Crohn's disease and recently had a surgery called an ileocolectomy (where a part of your small intestine called the ileum and a part of your large intestine called the colon were removed). This was done to create a new anastomosis (where the remaining ends of your intestines were joined together) after you had an acute perforative abdomen (meaning there was a sudden hole in your tummy organs). You were admitted today to a monitored bed (a bed where your vital signs like BP and heart rate are continuously watched) in the red room because you had hypotension (low BP), fever (high temperature), and had been fainting for one day.

You were recently admitted to [organization] to treat an intra-abdominal collection (a build-up of fluid inside your tummy), increased urinary output (more urine coming out) through your ileostomy (a surgical opening in your tummy that allows waste to leave your body into a bag), and worsening of renal function (meaning your kidney function was getting worse). You were discharged on 11/15 with a plan to take ertapenem (an antibiotic given to fight bacterial infections) 1 gram every day, given intramuscularly (as an injection into your muscle), for 4 weeks.

When you were checked, your blood pressure was borderline (meaning it was just at the edge of what is considered normal, possibly a bit low; a normal BP is usually around 120/80 mmHg). You were eupneic on room air (meaning you were breathing normally without needing any extra oxygen). At the time of evaluation, you said you had no complaints. You reported maintaining physiological diuresis (meaning you were passing urine normally) and had no complaints about it. You also reported that your ostomy (ileostomy) was working well.

Antibiotic treatment was started with vancomycin (an antibiotic given to fight serious bacterial infections) and meropenem (another antibiotic given to fight serious bacterial infections). You were then transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU - a special ward for very sick patients who need close monitoring and treatment) of [organization], under the care of the proctology team (a team of doctors who specialize in problems of the colon, rectum, and anus) who accepted you from the intensive care unit, {omitted}. You continued to receive meropenem and vancomycin. You also received KCL 6% orally (potassium chloride, a medicine given by mouth to replace potassium in your body). Your continuous medications included loperamide (a medicine to help control loose motions or diarrhea), calcium carbonate (a medicine to provide calcium and sometimes to reduce stomach acid), cholestyramine (a medicine to help reduce cholesterol and manage certain types of diarrhea), and muciloid (a type of fiber supplement that helps with bowel movements).

On 12/27/2021, you were discharged with a plan for a follow-up appointment. You are scheduled for hospitalization again on 01/22.
